newsitem.title: KENYA: New questions for African air safety after crash.
newsitem.headline: New questions for African air safety after crash.

text.p: For decades Ethiopian Airlines flew to become one of Africa's most respected airlines.
Run along U.S. management lines, its safety record matched the best in the world.

But this weekend's hijack drama that ended in the sea off the Comoro Islands not only tarnishes the reputation of Africa's flagship carrier, but once again raises question marks over the safety of flying on the continent.
The airline, exactly 50 years old, has boasted a proud record of success both under a 17-year Marxist dictatorship and the government led by rebels that in 1991 toppled the Marxist rulers.
But then on Saturday at least 67 people died when a Boeing 767, flight ET 961, crashed off the Comoro Islands after it ran out of fuel.
Fifty-two of the 175 passengers and crew survived and two Ethiopian hijackers were arrested, Ethiopian Airlines said.
The plane was hijacked after taking off from Addis Ababa en route to Abidjan via Nairobi, Brazzaville and Lagos.

Ethiopian Airlines promised a full investigation, but airline officials on Sunday were confident the airline would emerge unscathed from an investigation into whether the hijackers eluded airport security.
"This accident was not brought about by Ethiopian Airlines as such and it does not call the safety record of the airline into question," General Manager Ahmed Kello told Reuters.
"I would be very surprised if the hijackers could pass through Ethiopian Airlines security checks with guns and explosives since the checks are very rigourous," Kello said.
His optimism was backed up by reports from survivors who said the hijackers appeared virtually unarmed.
Until Saturday Ethiopian Airlines was rated not only one of the best, but also one of the safest in Africa, a continent criticised last week for its air safety record.
Nonetheless, Ethiopian Airlines flights had been hijacked previously -- nine times between 1991-1995 including at least four domestic flights and one international that took off from Addis Ababa.

African airlines conceded last week there were shortcomings in airline safety on the continent and said the situation would only get worse because governments were failing to impose tough enough standards.

The acknowledgement followed a report by the International Federation of Airline Pilots' Associations (IFALPA), which slammed African air safety, blaming pilots rather than ground crew for an increase in near-misses this year.

The African Airlines Association -- in a statement that could diminish confidence in African air transport -- blamed the problem on government failure to meet the minimum safety and operational standards required by established airlines.
But the Association defended Ethiopian Airlines on Sunday, arguing the crash had nothing to do with its safety record.

"This crash had no relation to air safety. The hijackers panicked and forced the plane to fly on until it had no fuel and that is why the disaster happened," director Aberra Makonnen said in a telephone interview.
Ethiopian Airlines was a rare bird that flourished in the face of Marxism as one of the few industries allowed to remain private by dictator Mengistu Haile Mariam.
In 1979, five years after Mengistu took power, the airline faced an $8.4 million deficit and looked in trouble.
But a decade later, using American management techniques, its finances allowed it to plan a 10-year, $1.3 billion deal to buy six new Boeing 757s over five years.
In the early 1990s, when Mengistu fell from power, the new regime replaced the airline's senior management, charging corruption and malpractice, a move that prompted fears standards would slip.
"There were changes in the early nineties, but Ethiopian kept up standards of staff, techical people, pilots and safety," Makonnen said.
Africa is no stranger to airline accidents. Five separate accidents in 1996 have left over fifty people dead.
